paragraph.text: M5. "I stopped being vegan because I'm at a different stage of life"

stages of life change what is easy, but they don't change what happens to animals. A stage with less time, more stress or other priorities is a good reason to ask for practical help, simplify the menu or do whatever is possible, not to treat a moral question as if it were a passing fad. No other moral commitment expires because a person has entered a new stage.
M. Ex-vegans: why I gave up ·
"I was vegan at one point in my life. Now I'm at a different stage; I have other priorities."
A person's priorities and availability change over the course of life.
It's reasonable to adjust personal choices to the priorities and availability of each stage.
Veganism is a personal choice, like any other.
So it's reasonable to leave veganism when entering a new stage.

P1 is true. P2 holds for personal tastes and projects. The problem lies in P3: veganism is about what is done to others, not a personal taste. Choices that affect third parties don't expire with the stages of life.
: P3 treats a moral question as a preference.
"Now, with a small child and work, it's not doable."
"I grew up and stopped being radical."
"It's hard; I don't have time." (which is J3)
"It's my personal choice; don't impose your morals." (which is E1)
When we grow up, our tastes change: toys, music, clothes. But some things don't change with age, like not hurting others. Animals still feel pain and fear, whatever stage of life we're in.

It makes sense that your life has changed, and that things are harder now. But the animals are in the same situation as before. If this stage has less time or more pressure, you can simplify: fewer recipes, more ready-made vegan food, and doing whatever is possible. A hard stage calls for adjustments, not for the question to stop mattering.
"What changed in your life, and did it also change the weight the animals had for you? Can you adjust what became hard without giving up what is still important?"
The argument mixes up two things that change in different ways:
What changes with the stage of life
The reasons that led the person to veganism

No one would say they stopped paying child support, being honest or not mistreating their dog because they entered a new stage. When a choice affects third parties, a change of stage can change how it's carried out, but it doesn't cancel it.

text.bold: 2. A hard stage calls for practical help.

paragraph.text: With less time, there are shortcuts: frozen food, packed meals, simple menus with rice, beans and vegetables. Real difficulty is a good reason to simplify, not to give up on everything.

text.bold: 3. "It was a phase" treats the reasons as a fad.

paragraph.text: If the person became vegan because of the animals, the reasons are still the same. What changed was the willingness to act on them, and that deserves to be said honestly (E15).

text.bold: 4. The most common cause is lack of support, not a change of values.

paragraph.text: In the Faunalytics survey, 63% of former vegetarians and vegans didn't like standing out from others, and 58% didn't see the diet as part of their identity. This suggests that many people give up because of social pressure and lack of a network, not because they started thinking differently.

text.bold: 5. Doing less is better than doing nothing.

paragraph.text: If the current stage really doesn't allow full veganism, keeping up whatever is possible (E10) still spares animals, and leaves the door open to coming back.
63% of former vegetarians and vegans didn't like standing out; 58% didn't see the diet as part of their identity; 84% weren't part of groups
Survey conducted in 2014 in the United States
37% of former vegetarians and vegans are interested in going back
(d) The strongest counter-reply: everyone has a limit, and no one should push themselves beyond it

The most serious version says: there are stages of life, such as illness, grief, a small child or unemployment, when a person can barely take care of themselves. Demanding the same of them as before is cruel.
(e) Why the counter-reply doesn't reach the conclusion

text.bold: Recognizing a limit is different from abandoning the question.

paragraph.text: In a very hard stage, it makes sense to do less, without guilt. That doesn't make exploiting animals acceptable.
The question is what to do when it passes: go back to what one did before, or keep the giving up as if it were permanent.

text.bold: The limit is rarely on the plate.

paragraph.text: In most cases, eating vegan takes little extra time when you have a simple menu.

Even if the current stage made everything harder, the question would remain the same: is it just to make animals suffer and die when it can be avoided? The answer doesn't depend on the stage of life of whoever is asking.
J3 "It's hard; I don't have time"
Lack of time is the concrete reason for the new stage
E15 "I know it's wrong, but I won't change"
The person admits the reasons still hold
E10 "Nobody's perfect; I do what I can"
E1 "It's my personal choice; don't impose your morals"
Veganism is treated as a personal taste
E14 "I admire you, but I can't do it"
Giving up turns into admiration for those who carry on
Treats a moral question as the preference of a stage
All or nothing, without considering doing what's possible
Talks about the eater's stage of life, not the animal

text.bold: Keeps other commitments at every stage.

paragraph.text: Honesty, caring for one's children, not mistreating the dog.

text.bold: The reasons are still the same.

paragraph.text: But the action changes as if they had disappeared.
But growing up usually means keeping commitments even when they get harder.
Going back to the norm relieves the discomfort of being different
The old habit seems like the natural state
Once they stop, the person goes back to not thinking about the animal
The principle being tested is: "commitments that affect others can be dropped when one enters a new stage".
It could stop being paid in a new stage
Lying would be acceptable in a hard stage
No one accepts this as a rule
It could be abandoned in a new stage

It's right that life changes, that some stages are genuinely hard and that no one should be held to account as if they always had the same availability. It's also right that guilt alone doesn't help anyone change.
But the stage changes what is easy, not what is right. The good answer is to help the person do what's possible at the stage they're in, and to remind them that the door is still open.
